Withholden
with-HOLD-en
v. (past part., archaic)
The archaic past participle of withhold, from with in its older sense of against or back, and hold. Webster 1828 records withholden alongside withheld. The form survives in the Authorized Version and carries a note of deliberate restraint.

Biblical Definition

Withholden is used of three things kept back — by God in judgment, by men in cruelty, and by nothing at all from God’s knowledge. God names His own withholding as a summons that failed: And also I have withholden the rain from you, when there were yet three months to the harvest: and I caused it to rain upon one city, and caused it not to rain upon another city (Amos 4:7), and the refrain through that chapter is yet have ye not returned unto me, saith the LORD. The drought was a message, precisely aimed and locally varied so that none could call it chance. Jeremiah traces a withholding to its cause in the people themselves: Your iniquities have turned away these things, and your sins have withholden good things from you (Jeremiah 5:25). Eliphaz uses the word to accuse Job of the cruelty of the comfortable: Thou hast not given water to the weary to drink, and thou hast withholden bread from the hungry (Job 22:7) — a charge that was false about Job but describes a real sin. And Job himself uses the word in his final confession, where nothing can be kept back from God: I know that thou canst do every thing, and that no thought can be withholden from thee (Job 42:2).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 gives WITHHOLDEN as an old participle of WITHHOLD: held back; restrained; kept back from action, from bestowment, or from use. Webster notes withheld as the more usual modern form.

expand to see more

WITHHOLDEN, pp. (old form) — Held back; restrained; kept from proceeding or from being given.

WITHHOLD, v.t. — To hold back; to restrain; to keep from action or from motion.

To retain; to keep back; not to grant; as, to withhold assent, or to withhold bread from the hungry.

To keep from any particular use or from a person who has a claim; hence, to defraud.

From with, in the old sense of against or back, and hold; compare withstand and withdraw.

Key Scripture

Amos 4:7 — "And also I have withholden the rain from you, when there were yet three months to the harvest: and I caused it to rain upon one city, and caused it not to rain upon another city: one piece was rained upon, and the piece whereupon it rained not withered."

Jeremiah 5:25 — "Your iniquities have turned away these things, and your sins have withholden good things from you."

Job 22:7 — "Thou hast not given water to the weary to drink, and thou hast withholden bread from the hungry."

Job 42:2 — "I know that thou canst do every thing, and that no thought can be withholden from thee."

Modern Corruption

Amos 4:7 says God withheld rain from one city and not another as a deliberate call to repentance, and modern religion has almost entirely lost the category of a providence that is aimed rather than merely arranged.

expand to see more

The detail in Amos is the point. God did not simply send a drought; He rained on one town and not the next, on one field and not the piece beside it, so that thirsty men walked to a neighbouring city for water and could not tell themselves it was weather. Five times in the chapter God lists a judgment — want of bread, withheld rain, blasting and mildew, pestilence, overthrow — and five times adds yet have ye not returned unto me. The Reformed doctrine of providence holds that God governs all events to His own ends, and Amos 4 shows that some of those ends are legible: a hard providence may be a summons. This must be said carefully, since Job’s friends drew exactly that inference wrongly and were rebuked for it; but the answer to their error is better discernment, not the modern conclusion that providence never addresses anyone.

Job 22:7 preserves their error for our instruction. Eliphaz reasons backward from Job’s suffering to Job’s supposed sin and invents specifics — that he withheld bread from the hungry and water from the weary — which the first chapter has already disproved. The lesson is not that suffering never speaks but that no bystander may assign its meaning to another man. Job 42:2 closes the matter from the other end: no thought can be withholden from thee. God’s purposes cannot be kept back by any creature, and no creature can keep a thought back from Him. That is the ground on which a sufferer may safely leave the interpretation of his affliction with God.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew mana (H4513), to withhold, to keep back; chasak (H2820), to restrain, to spare; batsar (H1219), to cut off, to restrain; Greek katecho (G2722), to hold back, to restrain.

expand to see more

Hebrew mana (H4513) — to withhold, to keep back; I have withholden the rain from you (Amos 4:7).

Hebrew chasak (H2820) — to restrain, to spare, to hold back; he that spareth his rod hateth his son (Proverbs 13:24).

Hebrew batsar (H1219) — to cut off, to fence in, to restrain; behind no thought can be withholden from thee (Job 42:2).

Greek katecho (G2722) — to hold fast, to hold back; the restrainer of 2 Thessalonians 2:6-7.

Greek apostereo (G650) — to defraud, to keep back by fraud; the withheld wages of James 5:4.

Usage

"I have withholden the rain from you (Amos 4:7) — a drought aimed field by field, so that none could call it chance."

"Thy sins have withholden good things from you (Jeremiah 5:25) — the withholding traced to its cause."

"No thought can be withholden from thee (Job 42:2) — nothing kept back from God, by any creature."
